name: Additions to Daniel: Bel and the Dragon
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of Bel and the Dragon in the version of Theodotion, as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which also prints the Old Greek (Septuagint proper, preserved in the Chigi manuscript 88 and the Syro-Hexapla) on the facing page; differences of substance in the Old Greek are given in the notes. In the Greek manuscripts the two stories close the book of Daniel; in the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles they are numbered Daniel 14 (verses 1–42 here match Dan 14:1–42). The Old Greek bears the title “From the prophecy of Habakkuk son of Joshua, of the tribe of Levi,” and calls Daniel a priest, son of Abal. Both stories mock idol worship (compare Isa 44:9–20; Jer 10; Jer 51:44, “I will punish Bel in Babylon and make him disgorge what he has swallowed”). The language behind the Greek, and the date (often put in the 2nd century BC), are uncertain. Bel and the Dragon is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes; dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton's English (1844), which translates the Old Greek, was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian received his kingdom.{a}
And Daniel lived as a companion of the king and was honored above all his Friends.{b}
And the Babylonians had an idol whose name was Bel,{c} and there were spent on it each day twelve artabas of fine flour and forty sheep and six measures of wine.
And the king revered it and would go each day to bow down to it, but Daniel bowed down to his own God.

And the king said to him, “Why do you not bow down to Bel?” And he said, “Because I do not revere idols made by hand, but the living God, who created the heaven and the earth and has lordship over all flesh.”
And the king said to him, “Do you not think that Bel is a living god? Or do you not see how much he eats and drinks every day?”
Daniel laughed and said, “Let no one mislead you, O king: this thing is clay within and bronze without, and never has it eaten or drunk a thing.”
And the king grew angry and called his priests and said to them, “If you do not tell me who it is that eats up these provisions, you will die.
But if you show that Bel eats them up, Daniel will die, because he has spoken blasphemy against Bel.” And Daniel said to the king, “Let it be done as you have said.”
Now the priests of Bel were seventy, besides their wives and children. And the king went with Daniel into the house of Bel.
And the priests of Bel said, “See, we are going outside; and you, O king, set out the food and mix the wine and put it out, and shut the door and seal it with your signet ring.
And when you come in early in the morning, if you do not find that Bel has eaten everything, we will die — or else Daniel, who is telling lies against us.”
But they were unconcerned, for they had made a hidden entrance under the table, and through it they would go in continually and consume the things.

And it happened, when they had gone out, that the king set out the food for Bel. And Daniel ordered his servants, and they brought ashes and sifted them through the whole temple in the presence of the king alone. And they went out and shut the door and sealed it with the king's signet ring and departed.
And the priests came in the night, as was their habit, with their wives and children, and they ate and drank everything up.
And the king rose early in the morning, and Daniel with him.
And he said, “Are the seals unbroken, Daniel?” And he said, “They are unbroken, O king.”
And it happened, as soon as the doors were opened, that the king looked at the table and cried out with a loud voice, “Great are you, Bel, and with you there is no deceit, not even one!”
And Daniel laughed and held back the king from going in, and said, “Look now at the floor and take note whose footprints these are.”
The king said, “I see the tracks of men, of women, and of children.”
And the king grew angry, and then he seized the priests and their wives and children, and they showed him the hidden doors through which they would go in and consume what was on the table.
And the king killed them and handed Bel over to Daniel, and he overturned it and its temple.{d}
And there was a great dragon,{e} and the Babylonians revered it.
And the king said to Daniel, “You will not say that this one too is bronze! See, it lives and eats and drinks; you cannot say that this is not a living god. So bow down to it.”
And Daniel said, “I will bow down to the Lord my God, for he is a living God.
But you, O king, give me authority, and I will kill the dragon without sword or rod.” And the king said, “I give it to you.”
And Daniel took pitch and fat and hair, and boiled them together and made cakes and put them into the dragon's mouth; and the dragon ate and burst open. And he said, “See the things you revere!”

And it happened, when the Babylonians heard it, that they were greatly indignant and gathered against the king and said, “The king has become a Jew! He has torn down Bel and killed the dragon and slaughtered the priests.”
And they came to the king and said, “Hand Daniel over to us; otherwise we will kill you and your household.”
And the king saw that they pressed him hard, and being forced, he handed Daniel over to them.
And they threw him into the lions' pit, and he was there six days.{f}
And in the pit there were seven lions, and they had been given every day two bodies and two sheep; but at that time they were not given them, so that they would devour Daniel.
Now Habakkuk the prophet was in Judea;{g} and he had boiled a stew and broken bread into a bowl and was going into the field to take it to the reapers.
And the angel of the Lord said to Habakkuk, “Take the meal that you have to Babylon, to Daniel, into the lions' pit.”
Habakkuk said, “Lord, Babylon I have never laid eyes on, and the pit I do not know.”
And the angel of the Lord took hold of the crown of his head, and carrying him by the hair of his head, set him down in Babylon above the pit, in the rush of his spirit.{h}
And Habakkuk shouted, saying, “Daniel, Daniel, take the meal that God has sent you!”
And Daniel said, “For you have remembered me, O God, and you have not forsaken those who love you.”
And Daniel got up and ate; and the angel of God at once returned Habakkuk to his own place.
And on the seventh day the king came to mourn Daniel, and he came to the pit and looked in, and there sat Daniel.
And crying out with a loud voice he said, “Great are you, Lord, the God of Daniel, and there is no other besides you!”
And he drew him out, and the ones who had been the cause of his ruin he threw into the pit, and they were devoured instantly before his face.{i}

notes.text: In the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles this book is Daniel 14. Astyages, the last king of the Medes, was overthrown by Cyrus about 550 BC; Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. The Old Greek has no such opening and begins, after its title, “There was a certain man, a priest, whose name was Daniel son of Abal, a companion of the king of Babylon.”
Bel (“lord”) is Marduk, the god of Babylon. Twelve artabas are about 19 bushels (about 670 liters); six metrētai are about 60 gallons (about 230 liters), as these measures are usually reckoned.
The Old Greek, as reported, says that the king handed Bel over to Daniel and that Daniel destroyed it.
Greek drakōn, a great serpent. The cult of a living serpent is otherwise unattested at Babylon; compare the mušḫuššu dragon of Marduk on the Ishtar Gate.
Compare Dan 6:16–24, where Daniel spends one night with the lions under Darius.
The prophet of the book of Habakkuk, of the late 7th century BC.
Compare Ezek 8:3. “His spirit” may be the angel's or God's.
Compare Dan 6:24. The Old Greek, as reported, ends with the king's praise of “the Lord God” and adds no further notice.
